author: Contributor 82
about: Larkspur, a twelve-person scheduling SaaS on AWS in us-east-1, over about eighteen months (journeys/customer-life.outline.md): its files in S3 from the applications it runs unchanged (the twin platform's nightly backups and a restore, its team's Rallly, its CRM Twenty with browser uploads behind the bucket's CORS, its team's LibreChat with presigned links and multipart uploads), and its secrets in Secrets Manager: the database credentials and the Stripe key moved out of environment files, a manual and then a Lambda rotation, a resource policy, replication to us-west-2 and a DR drill, an old key retired through its recovery window, quarterly audits, and everything deleted when Larkspur is acquired.

steps.name: Monday 5 January, 09:00: Larkspur keeps its files in S3, us-east-1
The World issues the applications' AWS access key (the IAM console's Create access key): Twenty, LibreChat, Rallly and the twin platform's backup job each sign with it
Dana's own access key, as she made it in the IAM console for her user dana (the platform team's)
Sam's, for his user sam (the platform team's, on call)
Dana makes larkspur-twenty-files, for Twenty's files
Dana makes larkspur-librechat-files, for LibreChat's attachments
Dana makes larkspur-rallly-files, for Rallly's images
Dana lists the account's buckets
Tuesday 6 January, 02:00: the twin platform's nightly backup
The backup job checks for its bucket: it is missing
and makes it
and puts the night's archive
Tuesday 6 January, mid-morning: Dana moves secrets out of environment files
Dana stores the production database credentials, which lived in the API's env file, as a JSON secret tagged with its team and environment

body.Name: larkspur/prod/db
body.Description: Production Postgres credentials for the Larkspur API

steps.name: Her CLI times out waiting for the answer and retries with the same client request token; Secrets Manager answers with the secret it already made

body.Name: larkspur/prod/db
body.Description: Production Postgres credentials for the Larkspur API

steps.name: Dana grants the API service's role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on larkspur/prod/db in IAM, an identity policy (docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/auth-and-access_iam-policies.html); an hour later the API is redeployed to read its credentials from Secrets Manager
STS gives the API service a fresh session of its role, larkspur-api, as it starts (session larkspur-api-1)
The API service boots and reads the database credentials
Dana stores the Stripe secret key the nightly billing job and the morning revenue report script need, tagged the same way, and in IAM grants each of their roles GetSecretValue on it

body.Name: larkspur/prod/stripe
body.Description: Stripe live secret key for the nightly billing job

steps.name: Wednesday 7 January, 02:00: the next night's backup
The backup job checks its bucket: it is there, in us-east-1
and puts the night's archive
09:30: a migration broke the test platform's state; an operator restores yesterday's
The platform checks its bucket
and lists the archives kept
It fetches the 6 January archive and writes its files back
Thursday 8 January, 14:00: the team's Rallly
Sam sets an avatar; Rallly's settings name the bucket larkspur-rally-files (a typo), and its upload route is refused
Dana fixes S3_BUCKET_NAME and Rallly restarts
Sam's avatar goes up through Rallly's upload route
His profile shows it through Rallly's storage route
Sam picks a different picture
The new avatar goes up
and Rallly deletes the old one
A page still holding the old link gets nothing
Monday 12 January, 11:00: Priya works in Twenty, the CRM
Priya uploads a prospect's logo; her browser's preflight to the presigned upload URL is refused: the bucket has no CORS rules

expect.contains: CORS is not enabled for this bucket

steps.name: Dana adds a CORS rule for the CRM's origin: PUT and GET, any header
The preflight now passes
Her browser PUTs the logo to the presigned upload URL Twenty gave it, which signs its type and length
Twenty moves it into the company's folder: a copy
then the pending upload deleted
Twenty stores the prospect's contract from its server
Dana tries Twenty in a sandbox workspace: an import file
and an attachment
Priya opens the contract through the presigned link Twenty gives her browser, naming its type, disposition and caching
Tuesday 13 January, 15:00: the team's LibreChat
A person attaches a PDF; LibreChat stores it
It signs a download link for the file, good for an hour and naming it as an attachment, and the browser opens it
17:00: the person opens the link again, two hours later
The link has expired
A call recording is uploaded in parts: LibreChat starts a multipart upload
its one part (the last part of an upload may be any size)
and completes it
LibreChat streams it to the person
The person deletes the PDF: LibreChat checks it is there
and deletes it
Ten minutes later the person deletes the PDF again from a second browser tab that still lists it
LibreChat checks it is there before deleting it: it is gone, so nothing more is deleted
Monday 2 February, 10:00: Dana deletes her Twenty sandbox workspace
First she opens larkspur-twenty-files in the S3 console, which lists it one folder level at a time: the CRM's workspace and her sandbox's
Twenty lists the workspace's files
and deletes them in one request
A Monday morning in February: the team is adding Redis
Dana stores the Redis auth token as a secret before the cache worker that reads it is deployed

body.Name: larkspur/prod/redis
body.Description: ElastiCache Redis auth token for the cache worker

steps.name: The next afternoon Dana grants the cache worker's role GetSecretValue on larkspur/prod/redis in IAM, and the worker is deployed
STS gives the cache worker a fresh session of its role, larkspur-cache-worker, as it starts (session larkspur-cache-worker-1)
The cache worker reads the Redis auth token on its first boot
A Thursday in March: a contractor who knew the database password left yesterday
Dana asks Secrets Manager for a new 32-character database password without punctuation, which the database driver mishandles
She stores it as a new version staged AWSPENDING, so the API keeps reading the current password meanwhile
She sets the new password on the database and checks a login with it
The login works, so she moves AWSCURRENT to the new version; the old one becomes AWSPREVIOUS, and AWSPENDING stays on the new one, as a finished rotation may leave it
That afternoon the API is deployed again
STS gives the API service a fresh session of its role, larkspur-api, as it starts (session larkspur-api-2)
The API service boots and picks up the new password
Early April: the first quarterly security review
For the security review Dana lists the production secrets by their env tag; none has been rotated by Secrets Manager yet (March's change was made by hand)
Mid-April: Dana locks the database secret down

Dana validates her draft policy that denies reading the database secret's value to everyone but the API service's role; the role ARN in its Principal is missing the account id, and validation refuses it
She puts the account id in the ARN and validates again; it passes
She attaches the policy, blocking any policy that would open the secret to everyone

Early June: Dana deploys the PostgreSQL single-user rotation function from AWS's template, with punctuation excluded, which creates its role with the Secrets Manager permissions the function needs on this secret
She adds the rotation function's role to the policy's readers, since the function must read the secret to rotate it
She turns on rotation every 90 days, the database team's policy, with that function, rotating once now; her token becomes the new version's id
A minute later: Secrets Manager has invoked the rotation function for create_secret
STS gives the rotation function a fresh session of its role, larkspur-db-rotation-role, as it starts (session larkspur-db-rotation-1)
create_secret: the rotation function reads the event it was invoked with: the secret, a new version token and a rotation token
It reads the current credentials to copy their connection details
As the template does before making one, it looks for a value under its pending version; Secrets Manager has made the version but nothing is in it yet
It asks for a new password without punctuation, as Dana configured it
It stores the new credentials under its version token, staged AWSPENDING, with the rotation token that vouches for its role
set_secret: Secrets Manager invokes the function again, with the same tokens
The function reads the pending credentials and sets that password on the database (outside Secrets Manager)
test_secret: the function logs in to the database with the pending password, outside Secrets Manager, and it works
finish_secret: the function looks up which version is current
and moves AWSCURRENT from it to the new version, which finishes the rotation
That afternoon Dana checks the schedule
She reads the secret's details: rotated at 10:00 today, rotation on every 90 days, the next due by the end of 31 August
At 09:00 the next day the API service is redeployed
STS gives the API service a fresh session of its role, larkspur-api, as it starts (session larkspur-api-3)
The API service boots and reads AWSCURRENT, now the rotated credentials
1 July: the second quarterly security review
Dana lists the production secrets for the review; the database secret shows it was last rotated on 2 June

September: an enterprise customer's contract requires cross-region disaster recovery
Dana adds the us-west-2 DR app's role to the policy's readers
She replicates the database secret to us-west-2; the replica is being made
Dana adds the replica to the DR runbook meanwhile
She checks the replica's status: us-west-2 now reads InSync
and that the replica carries the policy, so only the three roles can read it there
Early October: the third quarterly security review
Dana lists the production secrets for the review; new this quarter, the database secret is the primary of a replica, in us-east-1, and was last rotated on 31 August
November: the DR drill
Sam promotes the us-west-2 replica to a standalone secret, as the runbook says, with the platform team's IAM permissions, which include secretsmanager:StopReplicationToReplica
The drill's app starts in us-west-2 twenty minutes later
STS gives the DR app a fresh session of its role, larkspur-dr-app, as it starts (session larkspur-dr-app-1)
The drill app in us-west-2 reads the database credentials from the promoted secret
The drill ends that afternoon
Dana deletes the promoted copy without a recovery window; it was a drill copy
The next day, once the deletion has finished
Dana replicates the primary to us-west-2 again
She writes up the drill's findings meanwhile
She checks the replica's status: us-west-2 reads InSync again

Mid-January: billing moves to a restricted Stripe key
Dana stores the restricted Stripe key the billing job will use

steps.name: She grants the billing job's role GetSecretValue on larkspur/prod/stripe-restricted in IAM and points the job at it; its nightly run starts at 02:00
STS gives the billing job a fresh session of its role, larkspur-billing-job, as it starts (session larkspur-billing-job-1)

The billing run succeeded; Dana is in at 10:00
Dana schedules the old Stripe key for deletion with a 30-day recovery window
The next morning at 07:00
STS gives the report script a fresh session of its role, larkspur-report-script, as it starts (session larkspur-report-script-1)
A forgotten revenue report script still reads the old key the next morning and is refused: the secret is scheduled for deletion
Dana sees the failed report at 09:30 that morning
She restores the old key so the report runs until the script is fixed
That evening she reruns the missed report
STS gives the report script a fresh session of its role, larkspur-report-script, as it starts (session larkspur-report-script-2)

STS gives the report script a fresh session of its role, larkspur-report-script, as it starts (session larkspur-report-script-3)

Dana schedules the old key for deletion again, with a 30-day window
